analysis.one_liner: Taxes each stock, bond, and derivatives trade to fund public investments, with a credit for low earners.
analysis.headline: A tax on Wall Street trades that 37 House Democrats backed died in the Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a small tax on every transfer of stocks, bonds, and derivatives traded in the U.S. — half of one percent on stocks, a tenth of a percent on bonds, and a tiny fraction of a percent on derivatives. The money raised would fund infrastructure, health care, education, housing, and climate programs. Households making under $50,000 ($75,000 for couples) would get a tax credit covering whatever they paid through the trading tax.
analysis.who_benefits: Working households with modest incomes, who would receive a full credit for any trading tax they paid; communities that would gain from spending on infrastructure, Medicare and Medicaid expansion, student debt relief, low-income housing, and clean energy, funded by the new revenue [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 0.5% tax on stock and partnership-interest transfers, 0.1% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives, and excludes initial stock issues, municipal bonds, and very short-term debt [S3].

Gives a tax credit for the full trading tax paid by individuals with modified adjusted gross income up to $50,000 ($75,000 for joint filers), indexed to inflation, so the smallest households are held harmless [S3].

States that revenue would fund the social safety net, child care, infrastructure, expanded Medicare and Medicaid, education and student debt relief, housing assistance, transit, and clean energy and climate programs [S3].
States the tax's purpose includes curbing high-frequency trading, which may be up to 70% of the market and contributes to price volatility [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large securities firms, hedge funds and high-frequency traders who execute the most transactions; brokers and trading platforms would collect the tax; big institutional and wealthy investors would bear most of the cost, while most small households would be reimbursed [S3].

drawbacks.text: The tax would fall partly on ordinary investors through the cost of retirement funds and trades not reimbursed by the credit, though the bill's findings call the impact on the average investor negligible [S3].

Traders could shift activity to foreign exchanges outside the tax, since the bill covers only trades occurring or cleared in the U.S. or involving U.S. persons, and directs the Treasury to write rules to prevent avoidance [S3].
The tax could reduce market liquidity and trading volume, which would shrink the revenue base and raise costs for some investors — a standard objection to financial transaction taxes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is designed to place the cost almost entirely on high-volume financial trading while reimbursing households under $50,000/$75,000 in income, which keeps its burden off most ordinary people. The main real risks are that trading migrates overseas and that liquidity costs leak into retirement savings, so the projected revenue could come in lower than hoped. On balance the design is sound for its stated goals, but its scale — taxing the entire securities market — is exactly why it faced industry resistance.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which took no further action on it before the 114th Congress ended, so it never got a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on March 19, 2015 with 11 original cosponsors [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day; that was the only action ever taken on it [S1].
It gathered 36 cosponsors, all Democrats, but the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Securities firms and high-volume traders who would have paid the tax each time they traded, and who face no tax as a result of the bill's death in committee.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to create a financial transactions tax.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 19, 2015 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-led Ways and Means Committee never acted on it [S4][S1].

industries.industry: Securities trading firms and high-frequency traders
industries.note: The 0.5% stock tax and 0.005% derivatives tax fall directly on each transaction they execute, and the bill is explicitly aimed at curbing high-frequency trading. Their cost is the public's revenue source, so their interest runs against the bill's beneficiaries.
They would be responsible for collecting and remitting the tax on every covered trade, adding compliance costs, while also potentially losing volume as trading slows.
Swaps, futures, options, and other derivatives are taxed at 0.005% on payments and premiums, a direct new cost on a largely wholesale market that passes costs to end users.
Fund trades would incur the tax, potentially trimming returns, but households under the income caps would be fully credited, so most small savers would be made whole.
